  "research_question": "Does stimulation paradigm (Combined, ICMS Only, Dim Visual Only, Bright Visual Only, Sham) significantly affect mouse navigation performance metrics (Time-to-Target, Success, Path Efficiency, Average Speed, AD)?",
  "stim_paradigms_compared": ["Combined", "ICMS Only", "Dim Visual Only", "Bright Visual Only", "Sham"],
  "response_variables": ["Time-to-Target", "Success", "Path Efficiency", "Average Speed", "AD"],
  "anova_plan": [
    "For each response variable, perform a one-way ANOVA with 'Stim Paradigm' as the fixed independent factor to test for omnibus differences across the five levels.",
    "For 'Success' (binary, 0/1) and 'AD' (bounded [0,1]), verify normality; if violated, apply arcsine-square root transformation to AD and logit transformation to Success, or consider generalized linear models (GLM) as alternatives if transformations fail.",
    "For 'Path Efficiency', note the highly skewed distribution (mean 0.47 vs max 29.8); if normality cannot be achieved via transformation, use a non-parametric Kruskal-Wallis H test instead of ANOVA.",
    "For 'Time-to-Target' and 'Average Speed', proceed with standard one-way ANOVA assuming normality holds after checking diagnostics."
  ],
  "assumptions_and_diagnostics": [
    "Independence of observations: Verify that each mouse is treated as an independent experimental unit or account for repeated measures if the same mouse appears in multiple paradigms (currently dataset structure implies independent rows, but 'Mouse' column has 8 levels suggesting potential clustering).",
    "Normality: Assess residuals for each response variable using Q-Q plots and Shapiro-Wilk tests; apply transformations if necessary.",
    "Homogeneity of variances: Conduct Levene's test or Brown-Forsythe test across the five paradigm groups for each response variable.",
    "Homoscedasticity: Inspect residual plots to ensure variance is constant across all levels of 'Stim Paradigm'."
  ],
  "posthoc_plan": [
    "If the omnibus ANOVA F-statistic is significant (p < 0.05), conduct pairwise comparisons using Tukey's HSD (Honestly Significant Difference) test to control the family-wise error rate.",
    "If sample sizes are highly unequal (observed: Combined=48846, others << 12000), consider using Games-Howell post-hoc test which does not assume equal variances.",
    "Report effect sizes (e.g., eta-squared) for significant differences to quantify the magnitude of paradigm effects."
  ],
  "expected_findings": [
    "The 'Combined' paradigm likely shows superior performance (lower Time-to-Target, higher Success, higher Path Efficiency, higher Average Speed, lower AD) compared to 'Sham' due to multimodal stimulation.",
    "Sensory-specific paradigms ('Dim Visual Only', 'Bright Visual Only', 'ICMS Only') may show intermediate performance, with 'Bright Visual Only' potentially outperforming 'Dim Visual Only' if vision is intact.",
    "AD (angular dispersion) is expected to be lowest in 'Combined' and highest in 'Sham', indicating better path straightness in combined stimulation.",
    "Due to the massive imbalance in sample sizes (Combined n=48846 vs Sham n=3505), statistical power will be highest for detecting differences involving 'Combined', potentially masking subtle effects in comparisons between the smaller groups."
  ],
  "limitations": [
    "Severe sample size imbalance: The 'Combined' group (n=48846) vastly outnumbers other groups, making the omnibus test dominated by this group and reducing power for comparisons among the smaller paradigms.",
    "'Success' is a binary variable, violating ANOVA assumptions of continuous data; results depend heavily on the validity of the normality assumption after transformation.",
    "'Path Efficiency' shows extreme skewness (max 29.81 vs mean 0.47); this may indicate outliers or a distribution where ANOVA is inappropriate without robust methods or non-parametric alternatives.",
    "The dataset overview does not explicitly state the experimental design regarding the 'Mouse' factor (8 levels); if multiple paradigms were tested on the same mouse, a repeated-measures ANOVA or mixed-effects model is required instead of a one-way ANOVA."
  ],
  "recommended_next_analysis": "Conduct a Mixed-Effects ANOVA (or GLMM) treating 'Mouse' as a random effect to account for potential within-subject correlations, and use robust variance estimation to handle the extreme sample size imbalance and heteroscedasticity."
}
